intro: The largest singular value is the greatest amplification a linear map can apply to a unit-length input. Normalize that gain directly.
task: Scale a nonzero weight matrix so its largest singular value equals a requested positive bound.
requirements: weights is a nonzero matrix; bound is a real scalar in [1e-6,1000000]. Use the largest singular value from an exact SVD, not a power-iteration estimate.
Return {"weights": weights*(bound/sigma), "original_norm": sigma, "scale": bound/sigma}. This always normalizes to the bound, including when the original norm is below it.

Use finite real numeric values of magnitude at most 1e6, excluding boolean inputs. Each array axis has 1..64 entries and at most 65536 elements total unless a stricter bound is stated. Return NumPy arrays for array outputs, preserve caller inputs, and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: Diagonal gains
examples.output:
{'weights': [[0.75, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]], 'original_norm': 4.0, 'scale': 0.25}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 12 significant digits.)

examples.output:

hints.title: Follow the data
hints.body: The leading singular value measures operator gain, while Frobenius norm measures all squared entries.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: A zero matrix has no direction to normalize and is rejected.

explanation: Spectral normalization controls the worst-case Euclidean gain of a linear layer. It differs from normalizing each column or using the Frobenius norm, which can produce a different scale.
The bound concerns this linear map. Nonlinearities and compositions require separate reasoning; setting one layer’s gain does not alone guarantee a whole model’s robustness.
